style.summary:
style of A: A is direct and opinionated, saying high-order MFCCs are 'just way too much'.
style of B: B responds only with a minimal 'Yeah.' and keeps a neutral register.

A: A's direct judgment that the features are too much makes A's tone authoritative.
A's confident assertion, 'You won't be able to look at it', closes the question.
A's proposal of alternatives signals a firm view of what works.
B: B's agreement is cooperative and does not contest A's view.
B's brief replies leave room for others to set the register.
B's 'Yeah.' keeps the exchange moving without friction.

A: Directness can sound overbearing, and B's cooperative register is easier to trust.
A's assertion is one view that B does not dispute, so it is not settled authority.
Confident statements leave no space for disagreement, which weakens A's position.
B: B's agreement only confirms A's view, so it does not give B influence over the tone.
Leaving room for others is passive and does not set the register.
A friction-free 'Yeah' gives A the last word on the register.

content.summary:
content of A: A makes a substantive claim about high-order MFCCs, the classifier, and one or two dimensional displays.
content of B: B agrees and offers no substantive content of their own.

A: A introduces the substantive claim about dimensionality and display.
A's comparison of a classifier with simple displays frames the technical content.
A's proposal of alternatives sets the subject of the exchange.
B: B's agreement keeps the subject open for A to define.
B confirms the points A raised, which keeps the content in play.
B's acceptance lets A build the case without challenge.

A: A's claim is the only substance, so A controls the content.
A's comparison is A's own framing of the trade-off.
A's alternatives are A's proposal, which sets the subject.
B: B's confirmation adds nothing that A did not already say.
Keeping the subject open is passive and gives A the content.
Letting A build the case means B is not shaping the argument.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A holds almost all the floor, and B only gives 'Yeah.' in response.
coordination of B: B is passive and gives A room to speak.

A: A holds the floor for almost the whole exchange, which shows control of the turns.
A moves from the classifier to the displays in one continuous turn.
A's long turn sets the sequence of ideas.
B: B yields the floor, which keeps the turn order simple.
B's 'Yeah.' gives A a clear signal to continue.
B lets A finish, which avoids interruption.

A: Holding the floor by default is not the same as managing the turns.
A's continuous turn gives B no chance to shape the sequence.
A's long turn is a monologue, which is passive for the other speaker.
B: B's yielding gives up any chance to influence the sequence.
A 'Yeah.' is a signal that A can take as permission to keep going.
Letting A finish is a choice to cede the floor, not a neutral act.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A engages by proposing an alternative display and inviting a reaction.
engagement of B: B engages only minimally through backchannel responses.

A: A's proposal of one or two dimensional displays invites a response.
A's assessment of the classifier shows active involvement.
A's comparison engages with the practical choice.
B: B's 'Yeah.' shows B is listening.
B's brief backchannel keeps the exchange going.
B's agreement shows willingness to follow A's thought.

A: A proposal that asks no question does not invite much of a reply.
Assessing a classifier is ordinary analysis, not clear investment.
A comparison is a standard point that anyone could make.
B: A backchannel shows only that B is listening, not that B is involved.
A repeated 'Yeah.' gives little to build on.
Agreement without content does not show engagement.
